 Education Follow Unfollow Recent posts Opinion The great reckoning for American higher ed
 Perhaps it’s time to change the question from “Where are you going to college?” to “Should you go to college?”
 Follow Unfollow Recent posts By Tom Greene Follow Unfollow Recent posts Tom Greene is a syndicated columnist with deep roots in Alabama. He can be reached at [email protected]  or through his website at www.tomgreene.com. Published November 5, 2026 Read online: https://www.alreporter.com/2026/11/05/the-great-reckoning-for-american-higher-ed
 Listen Share Share article
 Bluesky X Facebook LinkedIn Email Copy link Print Bluesky Facebook Email Save Comments Questions STOCK Advertisement
 In the first nine months of 2024 alone, 28 degree-granting institutions  closed  their doors. Many were small or private institutions with idyllic settings for learning. The kinds of places that families embraced for generations.
 In 2026, American colleges are continuing the trend. See, the birth rate has been dropping since 2007, when an astonishing  4.3 million babies were born . Nearly two decades later, those kids represent the peak of college enrollment for a generation. It only goes “south” from here. The steepest  decline  (13 percent) will occur between now and 2028, when the freshman class shrinks by an astounding 320,000 students. On top of that, young adults are beginning to explore alternatives to college. But I think we are also witnessing something greater: the end of the great college spending spree.
 In a 2013 Gallup  survey , 70 percent of respondents said a college education was very important. Only 31 percent say it’s very important today. Much of that decline is a result of the exploding cost of education. It raises serious questions about the morality of burdening a teenager with a lifetime of debt on the hazy promise of a brighter financial future.
 Advertisement
 My tuition was around $1,600 per year at the University of Georgia in 1986. The all-in cost was around $5,000 per year. Since that time, tuition at all colleges and universities has exploded. Normally, when a business raises its prices too much, customers stop buying. College found a workaround: student loans. Thirty of the most expensive universities  cost  more than $72,000 per year. When you add in room, board and books, that can top $100,000 per year. Starting pay for a teacher in Cobb County, Georgia, is around $60,000 per year, or about $4,000 a month in take-home pay. Total loans of $400,000 will cost that teacher $2,300 to $3,300 a month for the next 25 years. That math just doesn’t “math.” A 17-year-old student couldn’t get a loan to buy a $28,000 Kia Sportage. So is it ethical to burden that same teen with enormous debt for a college education? People with bachelor’s degrees  earn  84 percent more over a lifetime than high school graduates. But those high school graduates won’t spend a lifetime paying off a college education that might not deliver the earnings to service that debt.
 Colleges and universities will argue that “almost nobody” pays the full cost of tuition. There are federal grants and local scholarships that help offset the high cost. Which raises another question: If almost nobody pays the sticker price, why is the sticker price so high? We wouldn’t tolerate this pricing model anywhere else, except when we are buying a Kia Sportage.

 Copy instruction Open ChatGPT (opens in a new tab) Perhaps it’s time to change the question from “Where are you going to college?” to “Should you go to college?” Suddenly, community college for two years doesn’t sound so crazy. Neither does a state university. Or a technical school. Or an apprenticeship as a plumber or electrician. Yes, the customer is finally beginning to shop.
 That’s potentially terrifying for small private colleges because many of them depend heavily on tuition. They have campuses to maintain, faculty to pay and dormitories to fill. A university can’t simply close half its campus because freshman enrollment drops unexpectedly.
 Advertisement
 Johnson & Wales University is taking note. It recently  announced  that it will offer three-year degrees in four fields at its campus in Providence, Rhode Island—computer science, criminal justice, graphic design and hospitality management. At $65,000 per year in tuition, that’s worth exploring.
 And after spending decades pretending they were invaluable, some colleges may be learning a painful lesson every other business eventually learns: You can raise the price for only so long before somebody finally asks whether what you’re selling is ethical or worth it.
